title: Hormuz Crisis and Building a Watch List
summary: Energy disruption and a selective watch list.
assessment: The shift toward prolonged-shock risk is justified, but the report overstates the global oil/gas share actually lost. Several watch-list names subsequently rebounded; those are useful observations, not claimed portfolio entries. Its strongest discipline is separating a valuation candidate from a purchase trigger and rejecting a single-episode safe-haven narrative.

claims.claim: One-fifth of global gas disappeared.
claims.reason: The gas denominator is incorrect: IEA’s roughly 20% figure concerns LNG, which is a subset of total natural gas. The adjacent oil statement is less clear-cut: blocked chokepoint export flows are not the same as net world production lost. IEA’s March 12 projection of an 8mb/d net oil supply decline predates the article and is a forecast, not a final observed March result. The gas error should not be used to dismiss the severity of the oil-flow disruption.

evidence.title: March 2026 oil market report
evidence.finding: IEA projected an 8mb/d March global supply decline, with offsets from other regions and emergency reserve releases; chokepoint throughput is not identical to net global supply lost.

evidence.title: Global LNG disruption
evidence.finding: Close to 20% of LNG supply was disrupted; LNG is a subset of natural gas. March global LNG production was 8% lower year over year after offsets elsewhere.
